items.title: After Binance, check what your signing systems can approve
items.summary:
Binance’s October 2026 security incident raises an operational question for every organization holding user funds: Can your security controls recognize when a valid signature grants an attacker wallet authority? If an organization only monitors transfers and ownership changes, it may miss the shift in wallet authority until assets move.

Binance’s initial update about the incident suggested that a compromised DevOps laptop allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawals. Its second update reported additional breaches but no evidence that wallet private keys had leaked. In its November 3 report, Binance described a broader attack involving social engineering, misuse of an internal AI tool, stolen credentials, and unauthorized access to its wallet-signing service. The attacker nevertheless obtained valid signatures, illustrating a major risk: a compromised server with permission to request signatures can misuse a protected key without extracting it.

The attacker used an EIP-7702 delegation that allows a wallet to sign a standing instruction: “Use this code when my account is called.” Ethereum keeps that instruction in place until it is changed or cleared using the wallet’s key. That enabled repeated transfers, including funds deposited after the first theft, without further signatures from Binance. Other Binance wallets were drained through ordinary signed transfers.

Transaction execution and monitoring systems must keep pace with Ethereum. EIP-7702 places delegation authorizations outside ordinary calldata. Session keys, recovery paths, authorization modules, Safe modules, and ERC-4337 UserOperations all add execution paths that signing policies and monitors must understand. Systems that have not been updated can miss malicious authority changes and asset movements, leaving wallets exposed. Teams must update their detection rules and test that these attack paths are covered.

If you’re responsible for securing wallet infrastructure, start with our checklist.

Four steps to strengthen wallet security

These four recommendations address the risks exposed by the attack. We also provide tests to help you verify that these security controls work.

1. Reduce access to signing infrastructure

Document every service and API that can request wallet signatures, who can call it, and what it can authorize, including transfers, delegation, and arbitrary data. Review this inventory whenever wallet functionality changes on supported chains. Separate signing infrastructure from everyday business systems and verify transaction details through an independent system. Use our TRAIL method to trace how a compromised laptop or server could reach signing.

Verify the result:

  • For each identified compromise path, use the access and credentials available to the compromised system to attempt an unapproved action. Identify the control expected to block it and retain evidence that no usable signature was produced.

2. Treat delegation as an administrative privilege

Configure signing services to recognize requests that change account authority. Reject EIP-7702 authorizations for custody externally owned accounts (EOAs) that do not need delegation, and ensure generic digest-signing APIs cannot bypass that restriction. Where delegation is required, separately approve the authorizing account, delegate address and code, chain, and nonce. Before evaluating execution, simulations must apply the proposed delegation and inspect changes to permissions and future execution authority alongside immediate balance changes.

Verify the result:

  • Delegation requests for accounts with delegation disabled are rejected through both dedicated and generic signing interfaces.

  • Changing an approved account, delegate, chain, or nonce requires renewed approval. Simulations expose added authority even when the transaction moves no assets immediately.

3. Limit damage even if signing is compromised

Even after delegation, the original EOA key can still transfer funds or change the delegate. This means that if the key is compromised, an attacker can bypass limits enforced by the delegate. Protect those assets with separate custody controls that the operational key cannot change. Our cold-storage guidance describes independently enforced limits, monitored delays on sensitive actions, and a separate configuration authority.

Verify the result:

  • Treat the operational key as compromised and attempt direct transfers, delegate replacement, and policy changes. Confirm these paths cannot bypass the claimed protections, including shortening or removing delays.

  • Exercise incident response against a malicious withdrawal. Record alert and containment times, and demonstrate that responders can cancel or contain the withdrawal before execution. Confirm that the blocked withdrawal cannot subsequently execute.

4. Detect changes in wallet authority

Map each wallet to the assets and contracts it controls, including wallets that hold no funds. Alerts should identify the affected systems and privileges (e.g., an unapproved delegation on an account that can upgrade funded vaults). Attribute direct calls, module execution, and ERC-4337 operations to their authorization paths.

Verify the result:

  • Test various delegation scenarios, mixed authorization tuples, multisig-module execution, and failed UserOperations inside successful bundles.

  • Monitoring should reconstruct authority changes and asset movements in order, identify affected systems, and distinguish detection from controls that block execution before funds move.

Make signing infrastructure an ongoing responsibility

If your organization runs wallets or signing services, take another look at how they’re secured. Test whether your signing policies account for EIP-7702 and ERC-4337, whether independent safeguards still work if an attacker gains access to signing, and whether your monitoring catches changes to accounts and permissions.

Give someone ownership of this review and put it on a regular schedule. Run it again whenever you change the protocols you support, the wallets you use, or your signing services.

items.title: The cryptography behind electronic voting (and why paper ballots are still essential)
items.summary:
As millions of Americans vote in today’s U.S. midterms, most will use paper ballots, which are protected by strict chain-of-custody protocols and, in some cases, statistical audits. You may wonder why we still use paper for our elections and voting systems when tasks like banking, tax filing, and document signing have moved away from paper-based legacy systems and become fully electronic. The short answer: security.

That may come as a surprise to some. After all, cryptography and other security advancements have enabled secure electronic systems for many applications. In fact, cryptography can be used to provide two essential safeguards in elections: keeping (1) individual votes secret while (2) making the final tally independently verifiable. This is exactly the approach of cryptographic protocols like Helios and ElectionGuard. However, Helios intentionally targets lower-risk and lower-coercion settings rather than high-stakes public elections. ElectionGuard, by contrast, is intended for public elections, but not as a replacement for a paper-based system; it is used as a cryptographic layer integrated with traditional voting infrastructure.

In this blog post, we’ll explain how cryptographic techniques can help protect ballot secrecy and prevent manipulation in electronic voting systems, and explore the limitations of these systems. Although cryptography can strengthen election verifiability and have other strong security properties, it cannot fully replace the security and trust of existing paper ballot systems in general elections.

The challenges of electronic voting

The National Academy of Sciences’ excellent 2018 report on election security concludes that electronic ballot return (also known as online voting or internet voting) should not be used in general elections, since “no known technology guarantees the secrecy, security, and verifiability of a marked ballot transmitted over the Internet.”

The difficulty of this problem makes sense when you consider the strong security guarantees any election system requires:

  1. Voter privacy must be maintained, even if a voter has a financial incentive to disclose their vote to a third party.

  2. Ballot integrity must be maintained. This becomes especially challenging in the electronic setting because, in general, the voter does not hold a cryptographic identity and cannot sign their ballot cryptographically. Oh, and the electronic voting client and server may be compromised anyway.

  3. Voters shouldn’t be able to vote more than once, but this is hard to verify without associating votes with their voters. This becomes even more challenging electronically when, again, voters often lack a digital cryptographic identity.

  4. Everyone should be able to trust (and ideally verify) that the election result correctly reflects the voters’ intent.

Paper-based voting systems must solve these problems, too. The first three requirements are typically met through standard physical security measures you see in paper ballot election locations: voters identify themselves to polling workers (preventing multiple votes from one person), are given a ballot without their name on it and a secure location to fill it in (protecting voter privacy), and personally hand their ballot to a polling worker and watch as their ballot is submitted for counting (ballot integrity). As with any security controls, there are threats that can compromise these protections; however, compromising them at a nationwide scale is extremely expensive, difficult, and noisy (i.e., detectable) to election observers, making these controls especially effective for large national elections. The final requirement is the most difficult to achieve for paper-based systems, and voters typically have to trust that election workers compute the final tallies honestly, and that chain-of-custody controls coupled with post-election audits would detect any attempt to compromise the election outcome. Cryptography can be used in conjunction with paper-based systems to help strengthen the trust in this final requirement, using what’s known as end-to-end verifiability, as we will explore later in the post.

Electronic systems introduce an existentially dangerous failure mode not present in modern, sensible paper-based systems: a supply-chain or 0-day vulnerability that can scale across many voting machines and jurisdictions could allow one person to single-handedly control and influence the outcome of an election (and, depending on the system and exact vulnerability, possibly while evading detection). In traditional paper-based systems, this risk is sharply constrained by independent physical records and physical security controls. It’s much more difficult for a single person to meaningfully change an election’s outcome while evading detection in this system.

Software security alone is not enough to secure electronic voting systems, though; the key design principle is not only to implement robust security controls but also to design your system so that all failures of those controls are detectable. This can’t be solved only using software whose correctness must be trusted. This property is known as software independence: changes in the election outcome caused by changes or errors (or vulnerabilities) in voting software must be detectable. In practice, this is typically achieved using evidence that can be verified independently of the voting software, such as a paper ballot audit trail.

Inside the design and cryptographic safeguards of electronic voting systems

Now that we’ve introduced the challenges of electronic voting, let’s explore how modern system designs aim to address them. We will focus our discussion on two electronic voting systems in particular: Helios and ElectionGuard. Helios is a complete voting protocol that targets low-stakes elections where coercion is not a concern. Famously, it is used by the International Association for Cryptologic Research to elect its board of directors. ElectionGuard aims to provide end-to-end verifiability on top of existing election infrastructure, and has been tested alongside systems based on paper ballots in College Park Maryland, Preston Idaho, and Fulton Wisconsin. Let’s look at how these systems use cryptography to provide voter privacy, ballot integrity, and end-to-end verifiability.

Protecting voter privacy

Encryption is a natural choice to preserve voter privacy and ensure that cast votes cannot be read by anyone else: by having the voting client encrypt ballots before they are returned, we protect them from being read in transit. But who controls the key we encrypt to? If we encrypt ballots to a public key controlled by the backend server, it could just decrypt each ballot when it is received, which would immediately reveal how users voted. (Even if the ballot is sent anonymously, the backend would still know how users at a particular voting station voted; it would just not be able to associate individual ballots with the corresponding voters.)

One way of solving this problem is to threshold-share the keypair used for encryption, and split the private key between $N$ trusted election officials. This means that a predetermined quorum $t+1\ \leq N$ of the trustees have to be involved in order to decrypt ciphertexts. Using a homomorphic encryption scheme offers further protection for individual encrypted ballots: it allows the backend to compute an encrypted tally from the encrypted votes and only decrypt the final result. As long as $N-t$ election officials are honest, this protects the confidentiality of cast votes from the voting client to the inclusion in the final tally1.

${{E}_{K}({x}_{1}+\ \ldots \ +{x}_{N})\ ={E}_{K}({x}_{1})\ \oplus \ \ldots \ \oplus {E}_{K}({x}_{N})}_{}$

With homomorphic encryption, the server can compute the encryption of the sum of the individual votes ${x}_{i}$ as the sum of the encrypted votes ${E}_{K}({x}_{i})$.

Schemes like Helios and ElectionGuard use a version of exponential ElGamal to encrypt individual choices on the ballot2. If the threshold-shared election key is $K\ =\ {g}^{k}$, the choice $x$ is encrypted as ${E}_{K}(x)\ =\ ({g}^{r},\ {K}^{r}{g}^{x})$, where $r$ is a random scalar. This scheme is additively homomorphic using pointwise multiplication of ciphertexts, as shown below.

${E}_{K}(x)\ \oplus {E}_{K}(y)\ {=}_{}({g}^{r}{\cdot g}^{s},{K}^{r}{g}^{x}\cdot {K}^{s}{g}^{y})\ =\ ({g}^{r+s},\ {K}^{r+s}{g}^{x+y})={E}_{K}(x+y)$

Exponential ElGamal is additively homomorphic if we define $\oplus$ as pointwise multiplication of ciphertexts.

Note that decryption yields ${g}^{x}$ rather than $x$, which is typically hard to invert. However, since $x$ is comparatively small in this case, we can use brute force (or tables) to recover the exponent.

As an example, if we use 0 to indicate No and 1 to indicate Yes, we can compute the number of Yes-votes by summing the individual encrypted votes as described above, and then decrypting the encrypted tally to reveal the result. However, if we don’t ensure that individual ciphertexts are well-formed, a compromised client could simply encrypt the value 1,000,000 to vote Yes a million times. To prevent this, clients must include a zero-knowledge proof ensuring that the encrypted ballot contains a permitted value (or a permitted combination of values).

Protecting against a compromised voting client

What if the voting client is hacked and alters the voters’ choices before they are encrypted, or drops the ballot completely? To protect against client compromise, the voter needs a way to ensure that the backend received their ballot, and that the choices recorded and encrypted by the software client correspond to how they actually voted.

This can be achieved in different ways. Helios and ElectionGuard use a mechanism known as Benaloh’s challenge method. The underlying idea is that when the ballot is encrypted, the voter obtains a commitment to the encrypted ballot and is then allowed to challenge and spoil their ballot. If they do, the ballot is opened and the voter can verify that their choices were recorded correctly and that the commitment corresponds to the encrypted ballot. The device has to reveal the commitment to the voter before learning whether or not the voter wants to challenge the encrypted ballot. Otherwise, it could present a correct commitment only when it is challenged. Moreover, it must be possible to obtain some external validation that the committed ciphertext actually encrypts the voter’s intended choices. Otherwise, the voting client can simply lie and present a plaintext that doesn’t match the commitment.

When the voter is satisfied that the voting client records their choices honestly, they record their choices one last time and cast their ballot, which is then published to a public bulletin board. The voter can use their commitment to check that their encrypted ballot is included in the published election record.

While this protocol provides a method to detect a compromised voting client that tampers with the voter’s choices or drops ballots, it still requires that a significant portion of voters exercise the mechanism in order to ensure that compromised clients are detected with high-enough probability3. Moreover, it does not protect against other types of compromise, like a voting client surreptitiously sending the voter’s plaintext ballot to a third-party server.

Additional issues must be solved in order for this method to be secure. One is the problem of voter authentication: how does the voting client ensure that the voter is eligible to vote, and how do we ensure that only one vote is cast? Additionally, there is the previously mentioned problem of coercion: how do we protect voters from being strong-armed into voting for a specific candidate or issue when voting stations may be spread out all over the world?

Authenticating voters is generally a difficult problem in countries (like the U.S.) that do not have a widely used national ID. However, there are options available for specific groups of voters. For example, some voting systems designed for overseas military voters use the Common Access Card to allow service members to identify themselves. Protecting voters against coercion typically requires that voters are able to vote without being supervised, which seems like a difficult problem to solve using cryptography.

Protecting against a compromised backend

What if the backend server is faulty or compromised by an attacker? With encryption, the backend aggregates the encrypted votes into an election record, computes the encrypted final tally over the encrypted votes, and then lets election officials decrypt the result. Encryption protects voter privacy, but it doesn’t stop the server from dropping, altering, or injecting votes into the election record. How could we allow voters to verify that this did not happen?

If the election record is public (and we can ensure that everyone shares a consistent view of it), voters can verify that their encrypted vote is included in the record using their commitment to their encrypted ballot, as described above. This provides a mechanism to detect a compromised server which attempts to drop or alter votes. Again, we need to rely on active participation from many voters to ensure that a compromise is detected, since a voter can only detect if their individual ballot has been dropped or tampered with.

ElectionGuard extends this idea to allow voters to detect a change in any of the ballots cast before theirs by chaining ballot commitments generated on the same device. Without chaining, the commitment is essentially computed as a hash of the voter’s encrypted ballot. With chaining, ballot commitments are chained as follows:

${c}_{1}=H({c}_{0}\ ,\ {B}_{1})$ ${c}_{2}=H({c}_{1}\ ,\ {B}_{2})$ ${c}_{3}=H({c}_{2\ },\ {B}_{3})$ $\vdots$

When ballot commitments are computed as a chain, the hash chain is published together with the election record. Here, ${B}_{i}$ is voter $i$’s encrypted ballot.

This means that any changes are propagated forward, allowing voters to detect tampering with earlier votes cast using the same voting client.

Detecting a compromised server that injects additional votes is more difficult and usually requires external data, like voter participation records, to solve. It is not enough to associate encrypted ballots with voter identities, since a malicious server could pad the election record with ballots corresponding to abstaining voters.

Once the election record is trusted, it is possible to use zero-knowledge proofs to verify that the final result is computed correctly from the published election record. Since anyone can compute the encrypted tally from the election record, we only need to prove that the final aggregate ciphertext was decrypted correctly.

What cryptography solves that paper ballots can’t do alone: end-to-end verifiability

Recall our fourth requirement for election systems, which we admitted was most difficult to achieve for paper-based systems: Everyone should be able to trust (and ideally verify) that the election result correctly reflects the voters’ intent.

This requirement is usually formalized in terms of end-to-end verifiability, which means that the following should be possible:

  1. Each voter should be able to verify that their choices have been correctly recorded.
  2. Anyone should be able to verify that the final tally is computed correctly from the election record.

Taken together, these two mechanisms allow voters to independently verify that their vote contributed to the election outcome, without relying on a particular piece of software or hardware (which may be hacked), or external observers (who may not be trustworthy). This property isn’t achievable in exclusively paper-based election systems without introducing some level of trust in humans/institutions overseeing the election. For example, without trusting anyone, how do you know what happens to your paper ballot after you and your vote both leave the voting location? The reason you won’t know this in an exclusively paper-based system is simple: in order to protect vote secrecy, when you submit your ballot to be counted with the other ballots, you intentionally break the link between your identity and your ballot.

Well, using cryptography, you can introduce a mechanism to verify that a cryptographic representation of your vote was included in the election record while still preserving voter privacy! This mechanism is exactly what was described above: encrypt the ballots and publish them to a public bulletin so that voters can privately check that their vote was both included and not tampered with. This allows you to enhance trust in existing paper-based election systems without compromising their security properties. This is the exact design choice behind ElectionGuard.

We won’t be replacing paper ballots any time soon

Helios and ElectionGuard both build on the ideas outlined above, but their use cases differ. Helios explicitly targets settings with low coercion risk and advises against use in high-stakes public elections. ElectionGuard, on the other hand, is built to provide end-to-end verifiability on top of an existing paper-based voting system. Neither protocol makes a general claim to solve the problem of electronic voting because neither achieves the security of status quo paper-based systems purely electronically.

There is widespread agreement among experts on election security that paper ballots are essential for protecting the security and integrity of general elections, and that likely will not change anytime soon. However, cryptographic techniques like the ones described in this post can still be used alongside paper ballots to improve trust in the election outcome by improving the result’s public verifiability and auditability.

If you’re using cryptography to build a new voting system, please reach out. We want to hear about it!

  1. A higher threshold is not always better. Helios requiring all trustees to participate to decrypt the election result caused the IACR to have to rerun their 2025 election after it found that one of the trustees had inadvertently lost their share of the key. ↩︎

  2. Helios and ElectionGuard differ slightly in how they implement encryption. Here, we describe the method used in Helios since it’s closer to standard ElGamal. ↩︎

  3. As an example, if a compromised voting client tampers with 1000 votes, and voters challenge one encrypted vote in one hundred on average, the probability of the attack remaining undetected would be 0.991000 ≈ 4.3 ∙10-5. However, it is also important to consider what recourse a voter has if tampering is detected. This determines whether they are apt to raise concerns, or simply shrug their shoulders and try again. ↩︎

items.title: Backporting security fixes at scale with Codex
items.summary:
Stable Linux releases lack existing security fixes because backporting them is time-consuming and often thankless work. We’re using Codex to reduce the backporting process time from days to hours per fix, empowering human patch reviewers to rapidly submit fixes for critical software like Ubuntu Long Term Support, Fedora, and the Linux kernel. By October 29, our project helped deliver fixes for 149 distinct CVEs into stable Linux kernel releases, and several fixes to Fedora and Ubuntu packages.

Deploying fixes to older software requires multiple steps, including adapting fixes to older code, checking dependencies, and ensuring the fix did not introduce new bugs. A single task (like tracking down a bug in a bad commit) can take a week or more of effort that no one sees or appreciates.

Our Codex workflow has reduced the human effort required to prepare and review fixes. Excluding project-specific initial setup, preparing and reviewing a straightforward backport takes about 30 minutes of human attention; a more involved case can take around three hours. The workflow’s approach is twofold: agents perform activities like identifying missing fixes, adapting patches, assembling validation evidence, running tests, and preparing submission packets, while engineers review the patches and submit them to maintainers.

Those estimates only cover patch preparation and review; regression testing and maintainer acceptance remain essential. But the reduced human commitment makes a substantial class of neglected security work practical to undertake. The patch backlog is large, but we now have a practical way to work through it.

Do we have to decide between stability and security?

Software has bugs, and we try to fix them when we can. The first place the fix happens is in the latest version of the software. Unfortunately, that’s often the only place where the fix happens.

Backporting is the process of getting a fix from the latest source code to older versions. Fixes for big-name, critical bugs are indeed often backported quickly. But for many other bugs, the backporting process never happens. It is easy to understand why: software packaging is often done by volunteers who are already overworked, and backporting is frustrating, thankless work that gets little credit or publicity. For open source projects staffed by teams of volunteers, backports are (understandably) a low priority. As XFS developer Dave Chinner once described, this work is “effectively a full time job” that simply goes undone without sufficient resources.

The lack of backports is a problem because almost no one runs the latest and greatest version of software that’s been freshly built with today’s code changes. People overwhelmingly prefer slightly older, more tested software packaged in “long term stable” releases. For example, about 95% of Ubuntu Linux installations are of the Long Term Support (LTS) variety. When looking at installed Linux kernel packages from Debian’s popcon, the overwhelming majority are based on older stable trees:

Users are faced with a decision: they can either stick with a stable, familiar version of software that has security flaws, or upgrade to a newer version that fixes those flaws but introduces other changes and new features they may not want.

Many people purposely do not update to new releases; I think this is entirely justified and normal end-user behavior. Just recently, I updated my Mac to macOS 27 and couldn’t use a printer that had worked flawlessly for years (until Codex wrote a new, compatible printer driver). Similar situations effectively require older software.

We should not have to make a choice between stability and security.

Thousands of known CVEs lack stable-branch fixes

A swarm of cyber-capable AI agents can cut through a network of stable, known-vulnerable software like a hot knife through butter. The scale of the problem is such that the software you are currently running likely contains unfixed security bugs that can be exploited by modern AI agents. As AI-assisted bug hunting makes it easier to identify vulnerabilities in older code, reducing this backlog becomes increasingly important. This is not merely theoretical. A fix for the latest high-profile bug, CVE-2026-98432 (a critical remotely exploitable flaw in the Linux TCP stack), still had not landed in distribution kernels weeks after being patched upstream. That bug is high-profile enough that it will soon be fixed everywhere. But fixes for more obscure bugs never get backported. I saw this during my sandbox escape research, and an old vulnerability in stable software was used as a part of the recently disclosed OpenAI hack.

Let’s quantify the scale of the missing backport problem. To make counting simple, we can limit ourselves to known bugs (with assigned CVEs) that are patched in the latest release but missing from stable packages. For this example, we’ll look at the Linux kernel, Ubuntu 26.04 LTS and Debian 13 Stable. I’m not singling out those projects—they are all run very well! I’m using them because they have documentation and accounting for unfixed CVEs. Other projects lack this transparency.

Let’s look at the number of outstanding CVEs in the Linux kernel, by stable branch. The table below shows CVEs per supported stable branch that do not have a fix in that branch, but do have it in a newer branch. (Hence, older branches by definition have more unfixed CVEs.) The source is the kernel CVE team’s vulns.git as of September 18, 2026. This is not an exact bug count, as it both over- and under-counts due to several technicalities. It is also not a measure of exploitability. Rather, it’s a measuring stick showing that a substantial amount of known CVEs have not been fixed in stable kernel branches:

Branch Unfixed CVEs % CVEs with an NVD Score High or Critical Severity
5.10.y 2,006 55.8% 213 (19.0%)
5.15.y 1,889 51.5% 195 (20.0%)
6.1.y 1,329 43.9% 99 (17.0%)
6.6.y 1,012 35.6% 65 (18.1%)
6.12.y 686 22.3% 21 (13.7%)
6.18.y 337 15.1% 3 (5.9%)

The package landscape is not any better. These are non-kernel CVEs reported as open or affected in Debian 13 and Ubuntu 26.04 (raw data via their respective bulk CVE data feeds, compiled by Codex). These are distro-metadata findings, not individually source-confirmed vulnerabilities. Again, this is not meant to be an exact bug count, but more of a measuring stick indicating how many unfixed vulnerabilities remain in stable software packages:

Distribution Source Packages with Unfixed CVEs Unique CVEs High or Critical Severity
Debian 13 1,128 4,562 1,822 (39.9%)
Ubuntu 26.04 1,028 770 335 (43.5%)

Engineers and AI can accelerate backporting

We realized this was an issue and have been fixing it proactively. First, we started with the equivalent of finding money on the sidewalk: there are bug fixes to known CVEs that apply cleanly to the stable kernel trees, but the fix was just never pulled into the kernel. We used Codex with GPT-5.6 to find these fixes, and asked the maintainers to apply the existing patches. They did, graciously. We then moved on to backporting patches that don’t apply as-is, starting with the most trivial to validate and review, and are slowly moving towards more complex changes. So far 149 CVE fixes in stable trees are currently applied; the list on our backport tracker just keeps growing.

We’ve done the same for Linux distributions: we used Codex and GPT-5.6 to identify known vulnerabilities in shipping stable packages, and then backport and validate a fix. We have begun reaching out to Linux distributions with an initial batch of patches.

If you run an open-source project or a Linux distribution and would like help backporting security fixes, please apply at trailofbits.com/patch-the-planet and we’ll be glad to assist.

The big upside of stable software that does not add features is that we can, in theory, fix bugs before attackers exploit them. So, let’s continue to patch the planet!

items.title: Your AI agent fixed the bug, but what else did it change?
items.summary:
Today we’re publishing patching-bugs and regression-hunt, two plugins that let engineers delegate patch development and regression checks to agents. Our patching-bugs plugin reproduces reported bugs, develops fixes, and tests them. The regression-hunt plugin checks whether any changes break previously working and supported behavior. Engineers can direct the work and review their results; maintainers can supply their own security assumptions and patching requirements, so the agents work within the project’s rules.

We built patching-bugs and regression-hunt through Patch the Planet, our joint initiative with OpenAI, where we’ve co-authored hundreds of security patches for widely used open-source projects. Motivated by our major successes on projects like Scapy, our plugins draw on our analysis of merged patches and thousands of our engineers’ Codex sessions.

The plugins provide maintainers with a structured workflow, evidence, independent checks, and best practices to improve their patching hygiene. In our preliminary evaluations, regression-hunt produces 25% fewer false-positive findings than a baseline Codex agent prompted to “review the PR for regressions.”

Standardizing the patching process

Our September post reported regressions introduced by some of our Patch the Planet patches. Since then, we’ve reviewed every patch that a Trail of Bits engineer authored and maintainers merged upstream. The review confirmed 21 regressions from over 130 PRs merged: 16 functional, one performance, and four build/test. None broke a security protection.

(“Regression” refers to a new defect introduced by a change that breaks previously correct and supported behavior along a path a real user or attacker can reach.)

For each patch, an agent looked for potential regressions, confirmed each one with a proof-of-concept (PoC) run before and after the change, and then passed the results to an engineer for review.

The review was noisy: today’s bug disclosures arrive at an unprecedented speed and scale, and for patching to keep pace, the industry needs to increase its signal-to-noise ratio. The 21 confirmed regressions were identified among 58 candidates in a single run (~36% precision). But because agents take many different approaches and reach different results, each run generates more candidates to manually sort through.

That led us to two conclusions:

  1. To introduce fewer regressions, we needed a standard way to write patches, with the same checks applied every time.
  2. To catch the regressions we still introduce, we needed a standard way to check for them, with written rules for what counts as a regression.

Standardizing both steps also makes every run repeatable and comparable. No fixed checklist will catch every regression, so we collect agent trajectories from our engineers’ patching sessions, and use the tasks that an earlier version failed to benchmark for the next one (figure 1).

How we designed the plugins

We used two primary sources to guide the design of our plugins: a review of every patch we merged upstream and the thousands of Codex sessions our engineers used to write those patches.

This led to four principles that shaped our patching-bugs and regression-hunt plugins:

  1. Opinionated guidance in as few words as possible. We give the agent wide latitude and record only Trail of Bits’ judgment of what constitutes a good patch and a real regression. The goal is to direct the agent towards the desired result with the least possible guidance.
  2. Modular steps. You don’t have to run either plugin end-to-end, as both provide multiple skills that can be used in tandem or in isolation.
  3. Strict input and output schemas. Every step takes and returns a defined schema that includes the claim, the code revision, the required check, the raw evidence, and open questions. Fixed schemas reduce variability across runs and allow each step to verify the previous step’s work rather than trusting its summary.
  4. A live proof of concept for every claim. Every conclusion depends on a PoC run against a live deployment: a built, running instance of the project, reached through the interfaces a real user would use. When reproducing a bug, proving a fix, and confirming a regression, if a step can’t produce a live PoC, its result is inconclusive.

regression-hunt reduces false positive rates

The regression-hunt plugin (Figure 2):

  1. Enumerates candidate regressions by tracing the changed code (the diff) through its callers to its real interfaces.
  2. Reproduces each candidate regression on a live deployment of the system.
  3. Replays the PoC on the live deployment on a fresh-context agent.
  4. Judges the results of all the previous steps to validate that the proof meets the requirements of a regression.

In addition to the four principles above, there are two core aspects that are critical to the plugin:

  1. Defining a regression: The plugin has strong opinions about what a regression is and, more importantly, what a regression is NOT. The burden of proof is placed on the agent (specifically during the “adjudication agent” step) to prove that there is sufficient evidence to show that the suspected regression is not a false positive, an incomplete fix, a latent bug, a pre-existing bug, and so on. The plugin only reports a regression if all of these gates are passed.
  2. Incorporating a threat model: If a threat model is available, the orchestrator will intentionally pass this document as part of the global context for each individual agentic step. This is an attempt to require each step/agent to refer back to the threat model before reaching its conclusion.

Our review of merged PRs yielded a set of 21 confirmed regressions that we could use to evaluate regression-hunt. We used the whole set to compare the plugin with a baseline Codex agent prompted to “review the PR for regressions.”

Across those runs, regression-hunt produced 25% fewer false-positive findings than the baseline, with a 95% confidence interval of 14% to 38%. Its strict evidence requirements also left some known regressions classified as borderline: the plugin identified a possible regression but did not gather enough evidence to confirm it. Fewer false positives therefore came with a tradeoff in how many known regressions it could confidently report.

Next, we’ll investigate why these cases remained borderline and improve the plugin’s strategies for gathering evidence. Our goal is to confirm more real regressions while giving maintainers clearer information when the evidence remains inconclusive.

patching-bugs streamlines best practices from thousands of agent sessions

The patching-bugs plugin is a distillation of all the best practices we’ve identified by analyzing thousands of Codex sessions by Trail of Bits engineers (Figure 3). In addition to the more traditional capabilities (such as reproduction on live deployments and independent adversarial review), the plugin emphasizes:

  1. The three-arm proof: The proof runs the same reproduction against three specifications: the original code must fail, the patched code must pass, and a complete revert must fail again. Bringing the bug back by removing the patch provides stronger evidence that the patch—rather than an unrelated environment or test change—actually fixed the bug.
  2. Invariant-guided repair: The patch attempts to fix the underlying, violated security invariant rather than fix the specific bug. This helps generalize the patch for possible variants of the same bug class.
  3. Incorporates regression analysis: The plugin mandates that regression-hunt is run to ensure that any patch goes through the same standard pipeline to check for mistakes.

What’s next for the plugins

Both patching-bugs and regression-hunt will continue to evolve. Our engineers are using them in their Patch the Planet work now, and we’re collecting data on how they’re being used, what works, and what doesn’t. That data, along with better evaluations, will shape the next version’s capabilities:

  • Evaluate patching-bugs. We’re building an evaluation that measures whether the plugin’s patches fix the reported bug and its variants without introducing regressions.
  • Learn from agent traces. We’re analyzing the first batch of trace-level data from our engineers’ sessions. It will show whether Codex follows the rules and definitions required at each step, which steps it skips, and where its evidence is weakest.
  • Make the plugins more configurable. patching-bugs already reads a project’s own patching guidelines (more on that in a bit). Next, we want maintainers to be able to choose whether to minimize patch sets—or, when broader coverage is worth more false positives, to loosen regression-hunt’s rules to surface more candidates.

These plugins encode best practices we’ve found for an agent to patch a bug properly, and they improve when you tell them how your project works.

The plugins work best when you input two kinds of project knowledge:

  1. A THREAT_MODEL.md, which tells agents what counts as a vulnerability or a regression. The regression-hunt plugin passes it to every step, so each agent has to check its conclusions against the file. It should define the following: assets whose compromise matters, trust boundaries, access controls, supported configurations, specifications on what is or isn’t a vulnerability, and evidence required for a valid bug report (example).
  2. A PATCHING_GUIDELINES.md (or AGENTS.md), which tells agents and patching-bugs how your project wants fixes written. It should outline how to build and test the project, how big a fix should be, where a fix should go, how to present proposed changes, and what a regression test must show (example).

For our Patch the Planet work with GPAC, our engineers wrote a threat model and a project-specific patching skill that captures how GPAC’s maintainers want bugs reproduced, what evidence a fix needs, and what a patch must preserve. Liboqs and validator.js have also published threat models in accordance with our guidance.

The more comprehensive and specific these files are to your project, code conventions, and operating style, the better the output you’ll receive.

The industry needs to focus on patching

As AI accelerates bug discovery, we need to turn those findings into reliable fixes just as quickly. Solutions need to balance speed and quality: an agent needs to understand a report, decide what needs to change, and check that a patch fixes the issue without introducing regressions. Our patching-bugs and regression-hunt plugins bring what we’ve learned from Patch the Planet into that workflow, helping maintainers move from a bug report to a patch they can confidently review and ship.

Install patching-bugs and regression-hunt, add a THREAT_MODEL.md and a PATCHING_GUIDELINES.md to your repository, and put them to work on your next bug report. Give the tools your project’s context so they can help you focus on the right fix and validate it faster. Then share your feedback, including comments about where our defaults don’t fit your project. Those real-world cases will help us build the next version.

items.title: Package managers have an integrity problem
items.summary:
I tested 25 of the most popular package managers to check whether they detect a compromised package repository injecting malicious code into legitimate packages. This code integrity problem could be solved using cryptographic hashes or signatures, but many package managers are still vulnerable to this threat. Of the 25 package managers reviewed1, fewer than half used lockfiles that checked for tampering by default, and only two verified the integrity of every package they downloaded.

Supply-chain attacks caused by developer compromise are a common story, but imagine what happens if ongoing mitigation attempts, including work by Trail of Bits2, are successful. If developers of popular packages are no longer the easiest targets, attackers will shift their focus to the next weakest link in the system: the package repositories that serve the code. The cryptographic answers to this problem are more subtle than they appear, and many implementations fall short due to deliberate design choices, resource prioritization, or the complexity of developer-friendly solutions.

One natural answer is to include a cryptographic hash of a package’s contents in a lockfile and compare hashes after downloading the package. This automatic verification was the default behavior in about half of the package managers I tested, but others required extra configuration to include or verify these hashes, used hashes in a cryptographically insecure way, or lacked hashes entirely. This is summarized in the following table.
Verifies integrity Go, vcpkg
Verifies if lockfile is present Bun, Bundler, Cargo, npm, pnpm, Poetry, SwiftPM, uv, Yarn
Verifies with lockfile + extra steps Conda, Gradle, Pip, NuGet, Pub
Does not verify with lockfile or N/A CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, cpanminus, Gem, Maven, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, R

Table 1: Lockfile-based security of a package manager fetching dependencies from a malicious repository, categorized by how much work it takes a developer to achieve integrity. Experimentally verified for a particular configuration. Caveats detailed below.

Another natural approach is to use signatures, avoiding the need to securely distribute a hash for every package. However, in my tests, only Go verified signatures by default; others required extra configuration, lacked verification code, or did not support signatures.
Verifies signatures Go
Verifies with configuration Bundler, Gem, Gradle, Maven, npm, NuGet
Missing or incomplete verification Bun, cpanminus, Pip, pnpm, Poetry, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, uv, Yarn
No signatures available for verification Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, SwiftPM, vcpkg

Table 2: Signature-based security of various package managers. Also experimentally verified and subject to similar caveats.

As both tables show, I found a surprising variation in the cryptographic designs and the level of protection they provide. Despite the challenges, I also found several communities on the frontier of this integrity problem that are bringing improved designs to reality. This post explores those variations, showing where certain designs fall short, why code integrity is harder to solve than it appears, and what cryptographic designs might be adopted in the future.

Simulating malicious package repositories

Studying the cryptographic behavior of 25 package managers is quite the challenge. I wanted to minimize manual analysis, but also be 100% confident when I claim an attack from a malicious package repository is possible. To solve this problem, I built a testing harness based on Docker containers and mitmproxy that dynamically evaluates the security of package managers against a malicious server.

The Ubuntu-based Docker images include a package manager, sample code, and optionally a lockfile. There are conflicting opinions about whether to include lockfiles in source code repositories, so I tested both configurations. The harness instructs the package manager to fetch dependencies from the repository, and the resulting network request routes through a WireGuard network to a custom mitmproxy addon.

Because the mitmproxy TLS CA is installed in the Docker image, the addon can fully manipulate the plaintext from the package repository, simulating a compromised server. I assumed any web-facing server could be compromised (e.g., Composer fetches metadata from Packagist and packages from GitHub), but backend resources, like any private signing keys, remain secure. The simulated repository embeds malicious code into the downloaded packages, and if the sample code executes the malware, the attack is successful.

I tried to keep the experimental setup reflective of real-world usage, but there are limitations. I installed the latest package manager versions, followed quickstart guides for setting up sample projects inside the container, and picked popular packages from public repositories to infect. I ran package manager commands with default flags to see if extra steps, like modifying the project manifest or running extra commands, were needed to enforce cryptographic integrity. However, I am limited to testing a single package with a single package manager version on a single platform, and the test conditions (e.g., PowerShell and CocoaPods on Ubuntu) may not represent the most common usage patterns. The setup isn’t meant to show that every developer is vulnerable to a malicious package repository, just that a developer following reasonable conventions is.

With the package managers installed and network intercept functional, one (mostly) promising observation is clear.

HTTPS is (almost) everywhere

Our harness architecture captures all network traffic, so it’s easy to test that package managers are using TLS and validating the certificates. In almost every package manager, they are.

The exception is cpanminus, the frequently recommended package manager for Perl. cpanminus uses unencrypted HTTP by default to connect to the Perl package repository, allowing any active network attacker to inject malicious code into downloaded packages. This vulnerability has been known for years, but the cpanminus developer has not switched to HTTPS, since doing so would be a breaking change to default behavior.3

Hash functions don’t always provide integrity

By using the mitmproxy addon to modify the package repository responses, I could investigate how different package managers use cryptographic hashes. Hashes are a natural way to ensure that a downloaded file has not been tampered with, but the main question is how the package manager learns the correct hash in the first place.

Microsoft’s vcpkg package manager for C and C++ libraries offers an interesting example. The package manager source code includes content hashes for thousands of dependencies. When a developer updates their library and wants to register the new content in vcpkg, they recompute the hash of their package and open a pull request against the vcpkg source code with the new hash and link to the package. When a package is downloaded by vcpkg, the hash is checked. So as long as the package manager is trusted, this approach is fully secure against a malicious package repository.4

Hashes in lockfiles

It is significantly more common that the package manager learns the correct hash via a lockfile. A lockfile is frequently created by a package manager, resides alongside a project’s source code, and references specific versions of dependencies needed by the project. If a developer checks a lockfile with cryptographic hashes into the source code repository, and the user’s package manager validates downloaded packages against the hashes, then the user’s dependencies perfectly match the developer’s.

This is how it works for the Bun package manager for JavaScript projects. Installing a package with bun add updates the bun.lock lockfile; committing the lockfile to Git and calling bun install on another copy of the repo verifies the hash in the lockfile against the new copy of the dependency. Similar behavior is found in npm, pnpm, and Yarn (also JavaScript package managers); uv and Poetry (Python package managers); Bundler (for Ruby); Cargo (for Rust); and SwiftPM (for Swift).

Other package managers support lockfiles, but with more steps than the standard add/restore process. Python’s Pip has experimental support for the pylock.toml format, and Conda has the optional library Conda lock. NuGet, the .NET package manager, generates a lockfile after adding the RestorePackagesWithLockFile property to the project.

Many package managers (Maven, R, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, and cpanminus) do not have dedicated lockfiles, and some have lockfiles (Gradle’s gradle.lockfile5 and Gem’s Gemfile.lock) without hashes in them.

Hashes present, but not for integrity

Surprisingly, I found a few examples where the lockfiles had a hash, but could still be compromised by a malicious server. This is not necessarily reflective of a vulnerability, since the underlying behavior is clearly documented, but it shows how there are multiple valid opinions about how lockfiles should be structured and consumed. Nevertheless, a user who is accustomed to the behavior of one package manager may be surprised by that of another.

The first example is the Pub package manager for Dart and Flutter. The following excerpt of a pubspec.lock file includes a SHA-256 hash for the uuid package.

If a user calls flutter pub get to fetch dependencies, Pub downloads the package from the pub.dev server and computes the hash of the returned binary. If there is a mismatch, Pub detects the error, but installs the package anyway.

This is documented behavior, and requires the non-default --enforce-lockfile option to block installation6.

Overwriting the lockfile after a hash mismatch was also the default behavior in pnpm until version 11.4 from May 2026, when it was changed to close “supply-chain holes.” Like Pub, pnpm also supported a non-default --frozen-lockfile flag, indicating that the previous behavior which updated the lockfile was expected.

Next, here is an excerpt of a conan.lock file, used by the Conan package manager for C and C++.

This includes the package name (zlib), the version number (1.3.1), a recipe revision cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20, and a timestamp. The 128-bit revision is an MD5 hash that includes source code. However, this hash is not intended to provide cryptographic security, but rather serves as a unique identifier. When Conan installs dependencies using this lockfile, it uses the recipe revision hash to download a particular file from the ConanCenter repository, but it does not recompute the recipe hash. Even if it did, there’s a separate package revision hash for platform-specific binaries that is not in the lockfile, and MD5 collisions could allow an attacker to create two distinct recipes with different behavior but the same hash.

The CocoaPods dependency manager for Swift and Objective-C has a similar pattern. Here is part of a Podfile.lock file for a project that uses the popular Files dependency.

This 160-bit checksum is the SHA-1 hash of the Files Podspec, which contains the following link to the source code. CocoaPods uses this link to fetch the Git repository.

So even though the lockfile can prevent tampering with the GitHub URL in the Podspec (setting aside expensive SHA-1 collision attacks), a compromised GitHub server could just serve a malicious version of the repository with the same tag.

Finally, the Composer dependency manager for PHP includes commit hashes in the composer.lock file, as in the following excerpt.

However, even though the b094ded... commit hash uniquely identifies the code, the ZIP archive in the URL does not include the Git tree as a way to verify the hash. Once again, GitHub could serve a malicious ZIP archive without detection by Composer.

Lockfiles have many roles besides supply-chain integrity

The previous experimental results show that lockfile hashes often can be used to enforce package integrity, but this is not their sole or even original purpose. Alternatively, they can lock dependencies to a particular functionality, enable an easy way for application developers to share a consistent environment, or facilitate reproducible builds. Analyzing package manager lockfiles through the lens of supply-chain security is a recent interpretation that can be at odds with their original design. The recent change to pnpm’s --frozen-lockfile is one example.

Another example of this tension is the question of whether the lockfile should be committed to version control. Most modern guidance recommends committing the lockfile for applications, since the final build environment is fully controlled. The question is more complicated for libraries, since package managers often ignore libraries’ lockfiles to avoid locking to conflicting transitive dependencies. Committing the lockfile makes it easier to develop the library by sharing a consistent build environment with other developers, but excluding the lockfile makes it easier to catch conflicts with different dependency versions before they are found by users. Many package managers recommend committing the lockfile for libraries (e.g., npm, pnpm, Poetry, uv, and Yarn), some recommend excluding it (e.g., Bundler), and some leave it up to the developer (e.g., Cargo).

Many of these questions are explored in a recent study by Gamage et al. The authors explore lockfile design decisions for seven package managers, analyze published projects, and perform semi-structured interviews with 15 developers. They find that the practice of committing a lockfile varies by which package manager is used, and categorize five benefits to using lockfiles, as perceived by the interview subjects: build determinism, integrity, transparency into indirect dependencies, debugging, and security scanning. Some of the developers also preferred to not use lockfiles, citing a preference for end users to resolve to the latest version of a dependency, which may have more bug fixes and vulnerability patches.

The diversity of package manager designs and views surrounding the purpose of lockfiles makes it difficult to prescribe a single recommendation. With regard to supply-chain integrity, it is common, but not universal, to view lockfiles as a source of integrity that should be committed with the source code. For package managers with lockfiles that do not provide cryptographic integrity, it is worth considering whether their users share that expectation. Even when lockfile hashes can provide cryptographic integrity, locking to specific package hashes means that users do not immediately receive subsequent updates or security fixes, since the newer package has a different hash. This leads to frequent lockfile bumping to distribute the latest hashes. Wanting immediate updates is a separate concern from wanting package integrity, but the current, common approach of using hashes in lockfiles is at odds with that goal. In conclusion, lockfile hashes are often, but not always, effective at providing cryptographic integrity, but do not work in every situation.

Signatures are common; verification is not

Signatures are a natural way to address these shortcomings, but implementations frequently fall short. In theory, developers could sign every release with their own private key, and the package manager could check the signature of the package it downloads from the package repository. In fact, signatures are relatively common in different package ecosystems, but proper signature validation is surprisingly lacking. The reality of using signatures to provide code integrity is more nuanced than it seems, and package managers have different approaches to the problem.

Many package managers have no signatures available. Arguably, vcpkg does not need them, because all package hashes are distributed with the manager, but this leaves Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, and SwiftPM7. The Conan developers are aware and previously decided not to fix it, citing several implementation challenges and suggesting organizations where integrity is critical could run their own repository server. Cargo developers are actively considering different signing designs, but this effort is still in progress. Composer developers have been implementing many new protections against supply-chain attacks, with future plans for artifact integrity.

Repository signing

One straightforward approach, known as repository signing, is when the package repository signs every package once it’s uploaded, and the repository’s public key is distributed with the package manager. This doesn’t solve the problem of a totally compromised package repository, since a malicious package repository could legitimately sign a malicious package, but it would protect against untrusted mirrors or a partial compromise of a package repository’s serving infrastructure.

Repository signatures are used by the npm Registry, the NuGet Registry, and the PAUSE server for Perl module distribution. In the npm Registry, signatures are distributed within package metadata with repository-specific public keys. NuGet Registry repository signatures are found in .signature.p7s files within the distributed ZIP package, again with repository-specific public keys. The PAUSE server takes a different approach, using its GPG key to batch sign the cryptographic hashes of several packages at a time.

Developer signing

Developer signing involves the developer maintaining the private key and signing the package before uploading it to the repository for distribution. This prevents the package repository from tampering with the contents, but it also provides a way for the package repository to authenticate the uploader.

There are two common approaches for a developer asserting their public key. In the first approach, the public key is distributed out-of-band. The Maven Central repository (used by Maven and Gradle) and the RubyGems repository (used by the gem and Bundler package managers) both support this type of developer signing. Maven Central uses PGP signatures, and developer keys are distributed by public keyservers. RubyGems uses self-signed certificates, and their distribution is left to the developers (e.g., rspec). The major difference is that developer signing is mandatory for Maven Central, and optional for RubyGems. Developer signing is rare for RubyGems, due to the lack of an established chain of trust, and a previous attempt to introduce a certificate authority failed.

The second approach involves a chain of trust. The NuGet Registry and PowerShell Gallery both support developer signatures. Neither makes signatures mandatory, but the PowerShell Gallery recommends it and the NuGet Registry has strict requirements if developer signing is used. In both, the developer’s key must chain to a trusted CA, and acquiring a valid code-signing certificate can cost hundreds of dollars per year. The benefit of this approach is that trusted root certificates can be preinstalled on the platform, allowing package managers to verify public keys.

One downside of developer signing is that developers are responsible for key management, and they can lose the ability to update their code if they lose access to their key.

Identity-based signing

An increasingly common middle ground is “identity-based” or “keyless” signing from Sigstore. Rather than require developers to manage long-term private keys, a developer can use Sigstore’s Fulcio CA to issue a fresh signing certificate on demand, for free. To prevent impersonation, the developer proves their identity with an OIDC token: a cryptographically signed statement from a third party like Google, Microsoft, or GitHub that attests to the email address, username, or potentially other claims about the developer’s identity. The verifier can check that the username is correct and the certificate chain links back to Sigstore Fulcio’s root certificate, proving that someone with access to that account created the signature.

Keyless signing is particularly useful because it can be integrated into a developer’s existing workflow-based deployment pipeline. This is frequently called provenance attestation or trusted publishing8. GitHub and GitLab provide OIDC tokens to Actions and CI/CD workflows that attest to the build workflow, the repository, and the commit hash. A workflow can use this token to obtain a signing certificate from Sigstore, sign the built package, and upload the signed package to the package repository. Since the signing certificate includes the commit hash and workflow details, this cryptographically links the built binary artifact to its source code.

Provenance attestation via Sigstore is supported by Python’s PyPI, the npm Registry, RubyGems repository, and Maven Central. While Sigstore attestations are not mandatory, there is already better adoption than RubyGems’ optional support for developer-managed signing keys.

Verification code is skipped, unconfigured, or nonexistent

Unfortunately, just because these signatures exist does not mean they are being verified by package managers.

In the npm package manager, the repository signatures are not checked when running npm install. Checking the signatures requires running npm audit signatures, which uses Sigstore to validate the registry public keys and then validates the signatures of the installed packages. pnpm recently added the pnpm audit signatures command, but that implementation fetches the registry public keys from the potentially malicious registry rather than verifying with Sigstore, so an adversary could simply add their own key and signature. Bun and Yarn currently lack an equivalent audit signatures command.

In the NuGet package manager, the default signatureValidationMode is accept, which installs invalidly signed packages. The user must set this to require and configure the list of trusted signers, such as with dotnet nuget trust source. These configurations (which include the repository public keys) can be securely distributed within a nuget.config configuration file, functioning as a lockfile that locks the trusted signers.

Ruby’s Gem and Bundler, and Java’s Maven and Gradle, which all use repositories with developer signatures, do not verify signatures by default. They require the user to manually add developer public keys (gem cert --add) or list the allowed public keys that should be trusted. In Maven, one can use the third-party pgpverify-maven-plugin with pgp-keys-map.list to specify the trusted PGP fingerprints. Gradle offers dependency verification, which works similarly.

Finally, several package managers seemingly lack any sort of verification code at all. Pip, uv, and Poetry do not currently have a way to verify identity-based attestations described in PEP740. cpanminus does not have a way to verify the integrity of the repository-signed CHECKSUMS file. It once did, but in response to a verification bypass vulnerability, this verification code was removed. Even though PowerShell is supported on non-Windows platforms, Authenticode signature verification is not9. At one point, the PowerShell repository noted that this issue “should be fixed in a future release.”

Go package management and transparency logs

Go’s built-in package manager is the only one I tested that verifies signatures by default, and it also introduces one final concept for cryptographic package integrity. When go get or go mod download fetches a package10, it hashes the package contents and compares the hash, package name, and version against the checksum database. The contents of the database are registry-signed (analogous to PGP signatures in Perl’s PAUSE server), and the default checksum database public key is hardcoded in Go’s source code. As long as the checksum database’s private key is used honestly, this design ensures that the package name and version are enough to uniquely identify the binary contents of a package. As a result, the go.mod lockfile achieves package integrity without needing to store cryptographic hashes.11

Go’s checksum database is an example of a transparency log, or an immutable, global, tamper-resistant log of metadata. The same capability is provided by Sigstore’s Rekor and certificate transparency logs. In package managers, it cryptographically ensures that the package manager only ever installs the same binaries recorded by the transparency log. If everyone agrees on the transparency log, then everyone agrees on the package contents. This makes it more difficult for an adversary to selectively and undetectably target a victim with a malicious package. Transparency logs can still fail if there are other vulnerabilities, the log’s private key is compromised, or no one checks the transparency log for malicious behavior.

Of all the package managers I tested, Go performed the best at maintaining cryptographic integrity in the face of a compromised package repository or proxy. However, the registry-signature-like design means that much of the system’s trust is concentrated in a single private key.

A proposed cryptographic design for package managers

One potential approach that combines the ideas in this post is to include signature information in the lockfile. Rather than commit to the hash of a particular package, the lockfile could commit to a developer’s identity or public key. This reuses much of the infrastructure in place for lockfile hashes, but it separates the question of immediate updates from the question of package integrity.

With this design, the lockfile could specify a single dependency version (for build reproducibility) or a lower bound (for immediate updates), and the included identity ensures that a malicious repository or proxy cannot easily tamper with whatever package version the manager resolves to. In addition, a transparency log can protect against selective targeting, building on Sigstore’s identity-based signing and transparency log service. Sigstore avoids long-lived keys by default, but it also supports self-managed keys, KMS providers, and hardware tokens. This gives an easily adopted and secure default while still giving flexibility to developers who desire more control over their keys.

This idea is not new and not my own. Attestation identities are part of the pylock.toml Python lockfile specification, the trusted-keys in Gradle’s verification metadata, and the pgp-keys-map.list file in the pgpverify-maven-plugin for Maven. This is the direction that many package managers are already moving towards, as evidenced by the increasing adoption of Sigstore into publishing workflows, attention on supply-chain security, and bugfixes that specifically cite potential tampering by a malicious adversary. There is increasing recognition that this is a problem, and increasing appetite to fix it.

It won’t be easy. There are many subtle nuances that have to be considered and addressed, signing verification code needs to be developed and audited, and developers need to adopt the resulting design. In many of the package managers I reviewed as part of this project, I found communities of people who have been thinking about and pushing for cryptographic integrity and package signing for years. They know best what those package managers need, and they deserve the resources to make this a reality.

One of the greatest cryptographic success stories in the past decade has been the nearly universal adoption of HTTPS, driven in part by industry and community recognition of the security risks of unencrypted traffic, and the nonprofit Let’s Encrypt providing free and easy-to-use TLS certificates as a public good. Package signing is in a similar state now to where HTTPS was a decade ago: persistent adversaries are a huge concern, and cryptographic security is nearly nonexistent. Universal package signing is not here yet, but it is on the horizon. With the right attention and investment, we can make it a reality.

Acknowledgments

Thank you to William Woodruff for valuable discussions about lockfiles, identity signing, and the challenges of package manager security.

  1. This post focuses on dependency managers for source code rather than system package managers like APT, Chocolatey, or Homebrew. The line between the two is blurred, but concentrating on one helps highlight particular usage and deployment patterns in that group. ↩︎

  2. Trail of Bits has several ongoing and completed projects to improve supply-chain security in some of these package ecosystems, including helping address both account takeover threats and the cryptographic integrity problem. ↩︎

  3. cpanminus is included in the default Docker container for Perl, but the container build scripts patch cpanminus to use HTTPS by default. ↩︎

  4. A subtle distinction here is that vcpkg must be updated using git pull in order to fetch the latest package hashes, shifting the question from securely installing packages to securely updating the package manager. For consistency with other package managers, we do not consider this question, and we note this as a limitation of our threat model. ↩︎

  5. Gradle can have a verification-metadata.xml file with content hashes, even though gradle.lockfile does not. ↩︎

  6. Note that some flutter subcommands, including flutter run and flutter test, call flutter pub get by default, so these commands can also overwrite the pubspec.lock file unless called with --no-pub. ↩︎

  7. The SwiftPM client has two main ways to download packages: via Git and via the custom Swift Package Registry Service Specification. The latter supports signatures, and the server protocol is implemented by private services such as JFrog Artifactory and AWS CodeArtifact. As far as I can find, there is no repository for the general public that implements this protocol, so I tested the signatureless Git format. ↩︎

  8. Trusted publishing can also refer to using OIDC tokens to authenticate to a package repository, and it does not necessarily involve identity-based signing. ↩︎

  9. Although I did not test PowerShell on Windows, the documented default ExecutionPolicy behavior is to block scripts on Windows client machines, and to require a valid signature for Windows servers. This achieves package integrity. ↩︎

  10. Go calls these downloadable artifacts “modules,” which consist of “packages.” For the sake of consistent terminology with the rest of the post, I use “package” in the general sense, not the Go-specific one. ↩︎

  11. The go.sum file stores hashes, but it is not a lockfile. Instead, it is a local cache for entries from the checksum database. ↩︎

items.title: SequenceHash: multihashing for the rest of us
items.summary:
Multihashing is one of those cryptographic tasks that’s easy not to think about too much. This is unfortunate, because multihashing is a common stumbling point when cryptographers try to use hashes.

As part of our goal to “fix software, not bugs,” Trail of Bits is introducing SequenceHash and its sister function SequenceMAC, a pair of related hash constructions that bring secure multihashing to developers using hash functions other than Keccak. We hope SequenceHash and SequenceMAC will help cryptographers avoid attacks that take advantage of ambiguous input encodings. The specification is open source, and is now a part of the Community Cryptography Specification Project (C2SP).

SequenceHash and SequenceMAC behave similarly to NIST’s TupleHash, but have the advantage of not being tied to a single hash function. They also don’t require developers to implement fiddly computations that aren’t byte-aligned. Instead, SequenceHash and SequenceMAC work out of the box with nearly any secure cryptographic hash function you care to use, including SHA256/384/512, BLAKE, and RIPEMD. SequenceMAC supports keys 32 bytes or longer (up to the ridiculous limit of ${2}^{128}-1$ bytes).

(It’s worth noting: SequenceHash and SequenceMAC rely on the security of the underlying hash for their own security. SequenceHash and SequenceMAC can’t magically make MD4 or SHA0 secure again. For the purposes of this document, it’s assumed that you have chosen a reasonable hash function like SHA256, not CRC32.)

To make SequenceHash and SequenceMAC easy to use, we’re releasing three initial implementations of SequenceHash and SequenceMAC: one each in Rust, Go, and Python. We’re also releasing a large set of test vectors that cover multiple hash functions and include intermediate values to help developers debug and verify their implementations.

Wait, “multihashing”?

Yeah, it’s a weird term, but the idea is pretty simple. “Multihashing” means “hashing a bunch of values together.” If you’ve ever read a cryptography paper, and there’s a step that says something like “compute the shared authenticator N=Hash(X, Y, Z, A, B),” that’s multihashing. You need to create a hash that incorporates the inputs X, Y, Z, A, and B. Unfortunately, the simple “solution” of concatenating the inputs and hashing the result can lead to serious security problems.

For example, consider what happens when you hash three inputs using “raw” SHA256:

This produces the following output:

Even though inputs are fed in through separate calls, they’re not separated from the perspective of the hash function—under the hood, the inputs are just concatenated.

As with many things in cryptography, multihashing is harder than you think. That’s a big problem because multihashing is a critical component of one of the most important tools in zero-knowledge proofs: the Fiat-Shamir transform. When you get multihashing wrong, you introduce the risk of forgeries into your zero-knowledge proofs. Given that zero-knowledge proofs play a major role in cryptocurrency nowadays, that sort of mistake is sometimes measured in millions of dollars.

But Fiat-Shamir transforms aren’t the only place where you might want to use multihashing. It’s not uncommon to need to hash a collection of related objects, where both the objects and the collection are variable in size. Think of authenticating the files in an archive, grouping multiple cryptocurrency transactions into a single hash, or hashing something as “simple” as somebody’s name.

Multihashing is also used when generating cryptographic commitments to values. In some protocols, one party must perform calculations using secret values, only to reveal them to other parties for later verification. Often, this is done by hashing the secret value along with a random “blinding” value and broadcasting the result to other parties as the commitment. If the boundary between the secret value and the blinding value isn’t clear, a “commitment” can sometimes be opened several different ways.

Unfortunately, nobody seems to have landed on a consistent, standard solution to this problem. Instead, across the open-source ecosystem and in our private audits, we find developers solving the problem in wildly different ways. Some of these solutions are insecure, like using separator characters that can also appear in the inputs. Others encode their data in a way that makes their separators unambiguous, but the encoding is unnecessarily complex and introduces subtle timing risks.
